items.title: What agents check at check-out
items.intro: The check-out report is measured against the check-in inventory, not against a hotel. Here is what comes up most often, and how to get ahead of it.

sections.heading: The standard is your check-in inventory
sections.text:
In England, a tenant has to hand the home back as clean as it was at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. Since the Tenant Fees Act 2019, a landlord or agent can't make you pay for a professional clean as a condition of the tenancy. What they can do is claim a reasonable cost from the deposit if the home is left dirtier than the inventory recorded.

So before anything else, find your check-in inventory and its photos. If the oven was spotless then, it needs to be spotless now. If it wasn't, that's in the report too, and it's worth knowing before you spend an hour on it.

sections.heading: Ovens, hobs and extractors
sections.text: The oven comes up on more reports than anything else, and it is the longest single job: about an hour for an oven in regular use, more if it has never been cleaned. Take the racks and the glass door panel out if they come out. The extractor filter above the hob is the one most people forget; a metal mesh filter can usually go through a hot dishwasher cycle.

sections.heading: Fridges and freezers
sections.text: Switch the freezer off the night before so it defrosts, with towels on the floor and a tray underneath. A freezer that is still frozen on the day can't be cleaned properly, and a wet one left shut grows mould within days. Prop both doors open when you leave if the inventory doesn't say otherwise.

sections.heading: Limescale
sections.text: Taps, shower screens, shower heads and the base of the toilet. In much of London the water is hard, so limescale builds quickly and doesn't wipe off: a descaler needs ten minutes or more to work. Never use a limescale remover and bleach together, or one straight after the other: acids and bleach release chlorine gas.

sections.heading: Inside, behind and under
sections.text: Agents open wardrobes, drawers and kitchen cupboards, and pull out what moves. Empty every cupboard, including the one under the sink. Clean behind the washing machine and the fridge only if they move safely; if they don't, say so in writing rather than force them.

sections.heading: Things that aren't cleaning
sections.text: Blown light bulbs, missing batteries in a smoke alarm, nail holes and a broken blind are usually listed separately from cleaning. Replace the bulbs, check the inventory for anything you were given, and leave every set of keys you received.

sections.heading: Take your own photos
sections.text:
When you finish, photograph every room, the inside of the oven, the fridge and the bathroom, in good light and with the date on the files. If there is a disagreement, your deposit protection scheme offers free dispute resolution, and it decides on evidence: the inventory, the check-out report and your photos. The rules on protecting and returning deposits are on GOV.UK.

We can't promise what a landlord decides. We can make sure the clean isn't the reason: if anything on our end-of-tenancy list was missed, tell us within 72 hours and we come back, free.

items.title: Keeping a home clean between visits
items.intro: Ten minutes a day, spent in the right places, make a fortnightly clean feel like a weekly one. These are the habits our cleaners notice in the homes that stay cleanest.

sections.heading: The bathroom, after each use
sections.text:
Squeegee the shower screen and tiles straight after each shower: thirty seconds, and limescale has nothing to dry onto. Leave the extractor fan running, or a window open, for fifteen minutes afterwards; damp air that stays in the room is what turns into black mould on the sealant.

A quick wipe of the basin and taps with a dry microfibre cloth before bed keeps the chrome from spotting. Hang towels open rather than folded, so they dry.

sections.heading: The kitchen, while it's warm
sections.text:
Wipe the hob as soon as it has cooled enough to touch. Fresh splashes come off with a damp cloth; the same splash a week later needs a degreaser and five minutes. Run the extractor whenever you fry, so grease lands in the filter rather than on the cupboard tops.

Empty the sink before bed and run the tap hot for a moment. Swap the dishcloth every couple of days and wash it hot; a sour cloth spreads more than it cleans.

sections.heading: Floors start at the door
sections.text: Most of the grit on a floor walks in from the street. A good mat outside and another inside, and shoes off at the door, cut the sweeping more than anything else you can do. A cordless vacuum by the door for a two-minute pass of the hall is worth more than one long session at the weekend.

sections.heading: Ten minutes, split
sections.text: Rather than one big tidy, try two minutes in each place: the kitchen surfaces after dinner, the bathroom after the evening shower, the living room cushions and anything left on the floor before bed, the hall on the way out in the morning. It adds up to ten minutes and nothing builds.

sections.heading: On cleaning day
sections.text:
Clear the worktops, the bathroom shelf and the floor. Our time is timed room by room, and minutes spent moving things are minutes not spent cleaning. Leave a note for anything you'd like done first; your cleaner reads it before they start.

If something is stained, broken or needs a different product, say so in the note rather than hope we notice. We'd always rather ask than guess on a surface we don't know.

sections.heading: Two safety rules
sections.text: Never mix bleach with limescale remover, vinegar or ammonia-based cleaners, or use them one after the other in the same toilet or sink: together they release harmful gas. Open a window whenever you use bleach or oven cleaner, and keep both in their own bottles, never decanted into something that looks like a drink.

sections.heading: The same cleaner
sections.text: You meet your cleaner on the first visit and they come every time after. They learn the home: which surfaces want which cloth, where the spare bin bags live, which door sticks.

sections.heading: Weekly or fortnightly
sections.text: Weekly visits are charged at a lower hourly rate than fortnightly ones and usually need less time per room. The strip on our home page shows both for your home. No contract: pause or stop with a week's notice.

sections.heading: Before regular cleans
sections.text: Many homes start with one deep clean, then regular visits keep it there. It isn't required; if your home doesn't need one, we'll say so.

sections.heading: After building work
sections.text:
Building dust varies too much to time from rooms, so we come and look, then quote. We clean in two passes a day apart, because fine dust keeps settling for a day after the first.

We need the builders finished, the rubble gone, and power and water on. We bring vacuums with filters made for fine dust.
